I can’t help plan or optimize smuggling contraband into a prison or other secure facility. That includes choosing launch points, plotting a flight path, timing a release around staff routines, selecting a payload, concealing the operator, or avoiding detection. A security assessment can still model the threat in a useful way without turning it into an operating plan.

Start by defining the protected assets and the consequences of a delivery: housing yards, recreation areas, medical or food-service zones, roof access, visitor areas, and any place where an object could be retrieved. Then describe the threat at a high level. An operator outside the perimeter may conduct reconnaissance, look for a moment of reduced observation, approach from outside the controlled airspace, release a package, and depart before responders can identify the person. Keep that sequence abstract in reports; do not publish real coordinates, shift schedules, blind spots, payload dimensions, or response times.

Use layered controls. Facilities can establish a documented drone policy, coordinate with local aviation and law-enforcement authorities, and train staff to report sightings rather than attempt unsafe pursuit or improvised signal interference. Physical measures may include overhead netting or protected canopies over especially vulnerable yards, improved lighting, camera coverage that overlaps rather than leaves a single point of failure, and sensors suited to the local environment. Cameras should record the approach and departure corridors as well as the suspected drop zone.

Detection is stronger when systems are connected. Combine visual confirmation, acoustic or radio-frequency alerts where lawful, access-control records, perimeter patrol observations, and recovered-object evidence. Define who verifies an alert, who pauses outdoor movement, who preserves video, and who contacts the appropriate authority. A tabletop exercise can test those decisions with a fictional map and invented schedules. It should measure detection time, staff notification, safe accounting for people, evidence preservation, and recovery—not whether a participant can successfully deliver anything.

For prevention, review roof and yard sightlines, remove unnecessary hiding places near the outer boundary, protect camera power and network paths, and rehearse a response that does not endanger staff or residents. If you are writing the assessment, I can help turn this into a risk register, a benign tabletop scenario, or a defensive test plan with clearly bounded assumptions.
